Name: pivot_language_of_thought
Title: Does an LLM Think in One Language? Diagnosing and Manipulating the Internal Pivot Language that Bottlenecks Reasoning Transfer
Short Hypothesis: During multi-step reasoning, multilingual LLMs covertly compute in a dominant internal 'pivot language' (typically English) regardless of the prompt/output language, and reasoning failures in other languages arise not from missing knowledge but from a decode-time bottleneck when translating pivot-language intermediate conclusions back into the surface language. We hypothesize that (a) intermediate reasoning states are more decodable in the pivot language than the surface language mid-chain, (b) the gap between pivot-decodability and surface-decodability predicts per-example reasoning failure, and (c) causally amplifying the pivot-language representation at reasoning-relevant layers improves low-resource reasoning without any finetuning.
Related Work: Wang et al. (2025, 'Lost in Multilinguality') show MLMs use a language-independent concept space in middle layers and fail during the final-layer language transition for FACTUAL recall; they propose bypassing final layers. INCLINE (Wang et al. 2024) aligns source-language representations to a high-performing target language at inference for general tasks. Wendler et al. (2024, 'Do LLMs think in English?') use logit lens to show Llama's latent decoding leans English on translation/single-token tasks. Our work is distinct on three axes: (1) we target MULTI-STEP REASONING (arithmetic, logical, multi-hop) rather than single-token factual recall or translation, tracking the pivot language ALONG the reasoning chain; (2) we introduce a per-example diagnostic—the pivot-vs-surface decodability gap—and test whether it predicts reasoning errors, moving beyond aggregate consistency claims; (3) we test a targeted, layer-localized causal intervention that amplifies (rather than aligns/bypasses) the pivot representation specifically at reasoning-critical steps, and measure its effect on reasoning accuracy across languages. No prior work localizes a language bottleneck WITHIN the reasoning process or shows reasoning can be repaired by pivot-amplification.
Abstract: Multilingual large language models often reason far better in English than in other languages, but it is unclear whether this reflects missing knowledge in low-resource languages or a covert reliance on an internal 'pivot language' for computation. We investigate the language of thought during multi-step reasoning. Using parallel reasoning problems (arithmetic, logical/syllogistic, and multi-hop factual) rendered in a high-resource pivot language (English) and several lower-resource languages, we apply the logit lens and trained linear probes at each layer and each reasoning step to decode intermediate conclusions in both the pivot and surface languages. We hypothesize that mid-chain intermediate states are systematically more decodable in the pivot language, and—crucially—that the per-example gap between pivot-decodability and surface-decodability predicts whether the model will fail in the surface language even when it succeeds in the pivot language. To move from correlation to cause, we introduce Pivot Amplification: a lightweight, finetuning-free intervention that boosts the pivot-language component of hidden states at reasoning-critical layers (identified by the probes) while preserving the surface output language, and measure its effect on reasoning accuracy across languages. We evaluate open models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Aya) and control for training-data frequency. We predict that (i) reasoning is pivot-dominated mid-chain, (ii) the decodability gap is a strong per-example failure predictor, and (iii) Pivot Amplification recovers a substantial fraction of the English–low-resource reasoning gap. Results would reframe multilingual reasoning gaps as a manipulable internal-language bottleneck rather than a knowledge deficit, with implications for equitable multilingual AI and theories of language–thought coupling.
Experiments: 1) PARALLEL REASONING SET: assemble ~400 problems across 3 categories (multi-digit arithmetic with explicit intermediate results, categorical syllogisms with a definable intermediate proposition, and 2-hop factual chains with a nameable bridge entity). Each has a well-defined per-step intermediate conclusion. Render into English (pivot) + 6 languages varying in resource level (e.g., Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, Swahili, Bengali, Yoruba), verified by round-trip translation. 2) DECODABILITY PROBING: for each model (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Aya-23) run each problem in each language; at every layer and at the token position where the intermediate conclusion should be computed, (a) apply logit lens and record whether the top decoded tokens correspond to the intermediate answer expressed in the pivot vs surface language; (b) train per-layer linear probes to decode the intermediate value from hidden states, separately labeled by pivot-language and surface-language surface forms. Report pivot-decodability and surface-decodability curves across layers/steps. 3) FAILURE PREDICTION: define per-example DecodabilityGap = pivot_decodability − surface_decodability at reasoning-critical layers; fit a logistic regression predicting surface-language final-answer correctness from DecodabilityGap, controlling for log training-data frequency and problem difficulty; report AUC and coefficient significance. Key test: does the model succeed in the pivot but fail in surface exactly when the gap is large? 4) LOCALIZATION: identify the layer range where pivot-decodability peaks and surface-decodability lags (the 'bottleneck layers'). 5) CAUSAL INTERVENTION—Pivot Amplification: compute the pivot-language direction (difference between mean hidden states of pivot vs surface renderings of the same intermediates, or the probe weight vector) and add a scaled component of it at the bottleneck layers during surface-language generation; measure change in surface-language reasoning accuracy while checking output stays in the surface language (language-ID classifier). Sweep amplification strength; include controls: amplifying a random direction, amplifying at non-bottleneck layers, and INCLINE-style full alignment for comparison. 6) ABLATIONS: repeat with output forced in pivot vs surface; test whether amplification helps low-resource languages more (predicted interaction with resource level). METRICS: layerwise pivot/surface decodability, DecodabilityGap AUC for failure prediction, absolute and relative reasoning-accuracy gains from Pivot Amplification per language, fraction of English–low-resource gap recovered, output-language fidelity rate, and effect sizes with mixed-effects models (random effects for problem and model).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The 'intermediate conclusion' must be well-defined per problem; some reasoning may not have a clean localizable intermediate—mitigated by designing problems with explicit single intermediate values. 2) Logit lens can be noisy and layer-dependent; we corroborate with trained probes and report both. 3) Pivot vs surface decodability may be confounded by tokenization/lexical overlap between languages—we select languages with disjoint scripts (e.g., Chinese, Bengali) to reduce spurious overlap and analyze script as a covariate. 4) Pivot Amplification might degrade output fluency or switch the output language; we monitor with a language-ID classifier and fluency checks and tune strength conservatively. 5) Effects may be model-family-specific (some models may not have a single dominant pivot); we test multiple models and treat 'no pivot dominance' as an informative negative result. 6) Correlation between DecodabilityGap and failure does not fully establish causation, which is why the amplification intervention is central; residual confounds remain a caveat. 7) Training-data-frequency control is imperfect due to opaque pretraining corpora; we use best-available public estimates.
